title: Calm & Mindfulness
description: Attention, calm and self-awareness through secular, age-appropriate practices: breathing, noticing with the senses, body scans, focus, gratitude, managing screens and sleep, and an introduction to contemplative traditions and the science of attention. Practices are optional, gentle and never forced.

goals: Take slow breaths using fun images

lessons.title: Balloon Belly
objectives: Do slow belly breathing using an imaginary balloon
Notice how slow breathing makes the body feel
prerequisites: Can sit still for a short time
explanation: Mindful breathing means noticing your breath. Put your hands on your tummy. Breathe in slowly through your nose and feel your tummy grow like a balloon.
Breathe out slowly through your mouth and feel the balloon go down. Try it three times.
Slow breathing helps our bodies feel calm and our minds feel clear — like letting a snow globe settle.
examples: Smell a flower (breathe in), blow out a candle (breathe out).
Bunny breaths: three quick sniffs in, one long breath out.

story.title: Pala's Bubble Breath
story.text: Pala the dolphin taught the little fish a game. "Breathe in slowly and fill your tummy like a big bubble," said Pala. "Now let it out slowly, slowly." The little fish who had been zooming around in a panic floated gently. "I feel calm now," whispered the smallest fish.

lessons.title: The Listening Game
objectives: Sit quietly and notice sounds
Describe what they noticed
explanation: Mindfulness means paying attention to right now, gently and kindly. One way is to listen very carefully.
Close your eyes (or look down), sit still and listen. What sounds can you hear? A bird? A fan? Your own breath? Count them on your fingers.
When your mind wanders off, that's okay — just gently come back to listening. Noticing helps us feel calm and focused.
examples: Hearing a crow, a scooter and a ticking clock.
Eating a raisin slowly and noticing its taste and texture.

story.title: Olu's One-Minute Quiet
story.text: Olu the owl said, "Let's be still for one minute and listen." Everyone closed their eyes. Kiko heard leaves rustling. Momo heard a far-away bell. Zuri heard her own heart. When the minute was over, they all felt peaceful. "The world is full of sounds we usually miss," hooted Olu.

activities.prompt: If your mind wanders off, you should…

lessons.title: Head to Toe
objectives: Do a simple guided body scan
Use tense-and-relax to let go of tension
explanation: A body scan is like a gentle torch moving slowly from your head to your toes, noticing how each part feels: warm, cool, tight, relaxed, tingly.
Tense and relax: squeeze your hands into fists for three seconds, then let go. Feel the difference. Try with shoulders, face and feet.
A body scan before bed can help you relax and fall asleep.

vocabulary.meaning: noticing each part of the body in turn

activities.prompt: A body scan can help us fall asleep.

lessons.title: Cloud-Watching Thoughts
objectives: Notice thoughts without getting carried away
Understand that thoughts come and go
explanation: Our minds are full of thoughts, like clouds drifting across the sky. Some are happy, some worried, some silly.
In mindfulness, we can watch thoughts float by without jumping on them. We notice, "Oh, there's a worry cloud," and let it drift away.
Thoughts are not always true. "Everyone hates me" is a cloud, not a fact. The sky — your calm mind — is always there behind the clouds.

vocabulary.meaning: an idea or words in your mind

examples: Noticing "I'm going to fail" as a worry cloud.

lessons.title: The Attention Gym
objectives: Practise sustained attention
Explain why single-tasking helps learning
explanation: Attention is like a muscle: it gets stronger with practice. Focusing on one thing — your breath, a candle flame (with an adult), or a sound — trains it.
Distractions pull attention away: phones, noise, wandering thoughts. Each time you notice and come back, it's like one "rep" at the gym.
Studies suggest that switching between tasks often slows us down and causes more mistakes than doing one thing at a time. Single-tasking helps us learn better.

vocabulary.meaning: doing one thing at a time

examples: Doing homework with the TV off.

lessons.title: Three Good Things
objectives: Practise noticing three good things each day
Practise sending kind wishes to self and others
explanation: Our brains often notice problems more than good things. A "three good things" practice trains us to notice the good: each evening, recall three good things from the day and why they happened.

Kind wishes practice: quietly wish "May I be happy. May I be safe. May I be healthy." Then send the same wishes to someone you love, to someone you don't know well, and even to someone you find difficult.
These practices, drawn from psychology and contemplative traditions, have been linked in some studies to greater wellbeing and kindness.

context.text: Loving-kindness practice (metta in Pali, maitri in Sanskrit) comes from Buddhist tradition and is now also taught in secular settings.
Research on gratitude and kindness practices shows encouraging but mixed results; effects vary between people.

examples: "A friend shared lunch, the rain stopped for play, Grandma called."
"May my little sister be happy."

lessons.title: The Science of Sleep
objectives: Explain why sleep matters for body and brain
Design a healthy bedtime routine
explanation: Sleep isn't wasted time — during sleep the brain stores memories, the body grows and repairs, and emotions are processed. Children aged 6–12 typically need about 9–12 hours; teenagers about 8–10 hours.
Too little sleep affects mood, attention, learning and health.

A bedtime routine helps: the same bedtime each night, a calm wind-down (reading, a body scan), a dark, cool room, and no screens for about an hour before bed, since bright screens and exciting content can delay sleep.

context.text: Paediatric sleep guidelines (for example, from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine) recommend 9–12 hours for children aged 6–12 and 8–10 hours for teenagers aged 13–18.

vocabulary.meaning: the same steps each night before bed
a hormone that helps us feel sleepy

examples: Reading a book instead of watching videos before bed.

story.title: The Test After the Late Night
story.text: Arjun stayed up late gaming before a test and felt foggy and grumpy the next day. Before the next test, he went to bed on time after reading and a body scan. He felt clearer and remembered more. "Sleep was studying I didn't know I was doing," he joked.

lessons.title: Screens on Purpose
objectives: Explain how apps are designed to capture attention
Make a mindful technology plan
explanation: Many apps and games are designed to keep us using them: endless scrolling, autoplay, rewards and notifications. These features grab attention, which isn't always good for us.
Mindful tech use means choosing why, when and how long to use screens. Before opening an app, ask: "What am I here for?"
Helpful habits: turn off non-essential notifications, use screens in shared spaces, set time limits, keep phones out of bedrooms at night, and take regular breaks to move, talk and play.
examples: Watching one planned episode, then switching off.
Turning off game notifications during homework.

lessons.title: Talking to Yourself Like a Friend
objectives: Explain the three parts of self-compassion
Replace harsh self-talk with kind, realistic self-talk
explanation: Self-compassion means treating yourself with the same kindness you'd show a good friend when things go wrong. Psychologist Kristin Neff describes three parts: self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness.

Self-kindness: instead of "I'm so stupid", try "That was hard. It's okay to make mistakes; I'll try again." Common humanity: remembering everyone struggles sometimes — you're not alone. Mindfulness: noticing painful feelings without ignoring or exaggerating them.
Self-compassion isn't making excuses. Research suggests it can help people learn from mistakes and keep trying, rather than giving up out of shame.

context.text: Self-compassion is a research area in psychology; findings are encouraging though still developing.

vocabulary.meaning: the words you say to yourself in your head

examples: "I failed this test" → "I'm disappointed. Lots of people find this hard. What can I do differently?"

story.title: The Coach in Your Head
story.text: Two runners missed a race goal. One heard a harsh coach in her head: "You're useless." She quit. The other heard a kind coach: "That hurt. Everyone has bad races. Let's look at what to train." She kept going and improved. The second coach wasn't softer on effort — just kinder about the person.

lessons.title: Meditation Around the World
objectives: Describe contemplative practices from several traditions
Distinguish secular mindfulness from religious practice respectfully
explanation: Many traditions include contemplative practice. In Indian traditions, dhyana (meditation) is one of the eight limbs of yoga described by Patanjali. Buddhist traditions include vipassana (insight) and samatha (calm) meditation; Zen emphasises seated meditation (zazen).
Christian contemplative prayer, Sufi remembrance (dhikr) in Islam, Jewish meditative prayer, and Sikh naam simran (remembering the divine name) are other examples.

Modern secular mindfulness, popularised by programmes like Jon Kabat-Zinn's Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (1979), draws on these practices without religious belief. People of all faiths and none can practise attention and calm, while respecting each tradition's own meaning.

context.text: In religious traditions, meditation is often connected to spiritual goals such as liberation (moksha, nirvana) or closeness to God, as understood by followers.
Jon Kabat-Zinn founded Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction at the University of Massachusetts Medical School in 1979.

vocabulary.meaning: a practice of training attention and awareness

All of them value stillness."

lessons.title: Evaluating Mindfulness Research
objectives: Summarise evidence on mindfulness effects
Identify limitations and hype in research
prerequisites: Understands study design and health claims
explanation: Many studies have examined mindfulness programmes. Reviews suggest modest benefits for stress, anxiety and some aspects of attention for many people — similar in size to some other well-established approaches.
Limitations include small samples, lack of active control groups (comparing with no intervention rather than another activity), publication bias, and over-enthusiastic media coverage.
Mindfulness isn't for everyone or every problem; for some people, intensive meditation can bring up difficult experiences. It complements, but doesn't replace, professional mental health care.

context.text: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses report small to moderate effects of mindfulness-based programmes on stress and anxiety, with calls for higher-quality trials.

vocabulary.meaning: a comparison group doing a different activity
positive results being published more often

examples: A study comparing mindfulness with an equally engaging relaxation class.

lessons.title: What Is the Self?
objectives: Compare views of the self from philosophy, religion and neuroscience
Reflect on personal identity
explanation: What is the "self"? Neuroscience suggests our sense of self is built by brain processes that integrate memory, body signals and social experience.

Indian traditions offer contrasting views. Many Hindu schools teach that the Atman — the true self — is eternal; Advaita Vedanta holds that Atman is ultimately identical with Brahman. Buddhism teaches anatta (anatman), that there is no permanent, unchanging self — only changing processes.

Western philosophy has its own puzzles: if every part of a ship is replaced over time, is it the same ship? If your memories changed, would you still be you? There is no agreed answer, but asking helps us understand ourselves and others.

context.text: Atman (in many Hindu schools) and anatta (in Buddhism) are religious and philosophical teachings held by followers; they are presented here for understanding, not to persuade.
Personal identity remains an open question in philosophy and neuroscience.

vocabulary.meaning: in Hindu thought, the true self
the Buddhist teaching of no permanent self
what makes someone the same person over time

examples: You at 4 and you at 14 — the same person?
The Ship of Theseus thought experiment.

story.title: The Ship of Theseus
story.text: An ancient Greek puzzle: a famous ship was kept in a harbour, and as planks rotted, each was replaced, until no original plank remained. Was it still the same ship? Students debated for an hour. One said, "Like my body — my cells change, but I'm still me. Or am I?"
